title: Four parts
hook: to Sigala: one part to live on, two for work, one kept for hard times (DN 31)
carry: enjoy some, build with some, protect some

segments.voice: Yesterday: anavajja-sukha, the happiness of blamelessness, which outweighs having, using and owing nothing. Blameless is best.

Early morning near Rajagaha. A young man named Sigala stands with his clothes and hair still wet, bowing in six directions: east, south, west, north, down and up. His dying father told him to, and he does it faithfully, without knowing why. The Buddha, walking into town for alms, stops and asks what he's doing. Then, gently, he reinterprets the whole ritual: the six directions are the people in your life. What follows is a whole sutta of advice for ordinary life, and somewhere in the middle of it, there's a budget.
screen: `WET HAIR, SIX BOWS.` → `HIS FATHER'S LAST WISH.` → `THE BUDDHA STOPS TO ASK.`

segments.voice: East is your parents. South, your teachers. West, your spouse and children. North, your friends. Below, those who work for you. Above, spiritual teachers. For each, the Buddha lists what you owe them and what they owe you. Then, in a run of verses, he turns to money. The wise person gathers wealth the way a bee gathers nectar, a little at a time, and it grows the way an anthill grows. Then the budget: divide your wealth into four parts. Live on one part and enjoy it. Put two parts to work in your business. Keep the fourth saved against hard times. It would still make sense on a spreadsheet. Notice what it assumes: a householder will have money, should enjoy some, should invest in their livelihood, and should plan for misfortune. Nothing here is otherworldly. The fractions don't map neatly onto a modern paycheck, and the tradition doesn't treat them as law; some read the two parts for work as money invested, others as the costs of running a trade. The shape is the lesson: enjoy some, build with some, protect some, and decide on purpose. The commentary, traditionally credited to Buddhaghosa, calls this sutta the discipline of the householder. Monks have their rules. This is a lay person's.
screen: `SIX DIRECTIONS, SIX RELATIONSHIPS.` · `LIKE A BEE, LIKE AN ANTHILL.` · `ONE TO LIVE, TWO TO WORK, ONE TO KEEP.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S DISCIPLINE.` · then, large: `FOUR PARTS.`

segments.voice: Without opening any app, picture your money in four piles, roughly as it is right now: the part you live on, the part that builds your work and your future, the part kept for hard times. Don't calculate; just notice the shape, how it feels in the body to look at it, and whether one small adjustment suggests itself.
Four parts. The Buddha's advice to Sigala: one part to live on, two for work, and one kept for hard times.
Your line: enjoy some, build with some, protect some. One for living, two for work, one for the rainy day. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Sigalovada Sutta is widely taught to lay Buddhists, especially in Theravada countries, as practical guidance for family, friendship, work and money.

chat.says: Did the Buddha ever give advice about money?
options: Yes: live on one part in four, put two to work, keep one for hard times.
Yes: save three parts in four, and spend only what's left on yourself.
Yes: split it equally between your family, your work and charity.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut the uncited age ('two and a half thousand years old'); attributed 'the householder's discipline' to the commentary traditionally credited to Buddhaghosa and dropped 'great'.
DN 31 paraphrased. Rhys Davids's translation (Dialogues of the Buddha III, 1921) exists but was not quoted because its exact wording could not be confirmed.
Setting: the sutta places Sigala near Rajagaha, bowing with wet clothes and hair; confirm.
Six directions mapping: east parents, south teachers, west wife and children, north friends, nadir servants/workers, zenith ascetics and brahmins. Script says 'spiritual teachers' for the last.
Bee and anthill simile and the four-part verse (catudhā vibhaje bhoge) given from memory.
Buddhaghosa's description of DN 31 as gihi-vinaya: confirm.
